clue.text: Send chaps abroad to 6's capital by carriage

indicators.note: a capital is the letter that heads a word, so only the opening letter of that entry is wanted

blocks.note: to send chaps out of the country is to deport men
the entry at 6 across, THAI

explanation.surface: Someone is having men shipped off abroad to a capital city, travelling by carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 6's capital means the first letter of the answer at 6 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Deportment is the way a person holds and carries themselves, their bearing or posture, which is also called carriage.

clue.text: Film about the home?

blocks.note: surface reading: a movie whose subject is domestic life
setter's reading: a thin grey layer lying all about the house, settled on every shelf

explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests cinema, and 'about' suggests a topic; read instead as a thin coating spread around a house.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine powdery layer that settles on furniture and shelves throughout a house is a film in the sense of a thin coating.

clue.text: Liquidity merger

definitions.note: a noun for a body of liquid; loosely, a puddle or pond

blocks.note: first meaning: a still body of liquid, as of water
second meaning: a combining of resources or businesses into one common fund

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like company finance, where liquidity means available cash; one meaning is a body of water, the other a combined fund.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool is standing water, and to pool resources is to combine them, so the noun also names a joint arrangement of firms.

clue.text: Tory hire call put out in orotund manner

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or upset, so the preceding letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician's call for hiring is delivered in a pompous, booming voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund speech is grandiloquent and pompous, the style of a speaker using rhetoric for effect rather than plain statement.

clue.text: Sound of cattle half seen — large deer

indicators.note: taking half of a word means the back two of its four letters are dropped

blocks.note: the lowing noise a cow makes
taken as written, before it is halved

explanation.surface: A lowing herd is only half glimpsed, and among it stands a big deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound of' here is the noise cattle make, not a signal that something is heard as another word.
explanation.definitionFit: The moose is the largest member of the deer family, called an elk in Europe, so it is a large deer by species.

clue.text: Guide found by pointers?

blocks.note: surface reading: a leader that hunting dogs, the pointers, track down
setter's reading: a navigator's star located using the Pointers, two stars of the Plough that line up with it

explanation.walkthrough: Pointers are gun dogs, but the Pointers are also the two stars at the end of the Plough (Big Dipper) whose line leads the eye to the pole star.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris has guided navigators for centuries because it stays fixed above the pole, and the Pointers in the Plough lead to it.

clue.text: Speech announcing dead heat

indicators.note: announcing something means saying it out to listeners, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a dead heat is a race that ends level, a tie

explanation.surface: A race commentator's speech declares the finish a dead heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Thai is the national language of Thailand, and speech can mean a language or tongue spoken by a people.

clue.text: Leader in queue also knows about service

definitions.note: a description of the person, a verb phrase for a noun answer

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: the person waiting at the front of a line
second meaning: the restaurant's chief server, an expert on serving diners

explanation.surface: The person at the front of the queue also happens to know a lot about service.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning splits the answer into its two words: the head (front) person who is waiting.
explanation.definitionFit: The head waiter runs the dining room and supervises the other staff, so he is the one who knows all about table service.

clue.text: Small distance on lines - speed is excessive

blocks.note: one millimetre, written as the Roman numeral I and the abbreviation mm
an ode is a poem, a set of lines of verse
a rate is a speed, as in the rate of travel

explanation.surface: A short distance covered on railway lines, at a speed that is too high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' suggests railway track, but it is verse; in a down clue 'on' simply places one piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Immoderate means lacking moderation, going beyond reasonable limits, which is what excessive also says.

clue.text: Music directorate runs register

blocks.note: a score is the written music of a piece
a board of directors

explanation.surface: A music directorate runs a register, as if an orchestra's governing body kept the roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs register' looks like a verb with its object; it is a noun phrase, something that registers the runs in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: At a cricket ground the board displaying the score records each run as it is made, so it is literally a register of runs.

clue.text: Conceal sign of victory

blocks.note: first meaning: to hide in the hand, as a conjuror does with a card
second meaning: the frond awarded to a winner in ancient times

explanation.walkthrough: A palm branch was carried as an emblem of triumph, hence the phrase bear the palm.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror hides a coin or card in the hand, and a branch of the tree was the classical emblem awarded to winners.

clue.text: Diet in a smart new way to control things

indicators.note: arranging something in a new way means the preceding letters are set out in a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone goes on a diet in a smart new fashion in order to take charge of their life.
explanation.definitionFit: To administrate is to manage or run affairs, an organisation or a process, which means keeping things under control.

clue.text: Presaged like Campbell's coming events

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase; the answer read as a past participle

blocks.note: first meaning: indicated in advance, gave warning of
second meaning: Thomas Campbell wrote in Lochiel's Warning that coming events cast their shadows before

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Campbell was a Scottish poet; his line 'coming events cast their shadows before' supplies the second, literal reading of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To foreshadow is to hint at something before it happens, and Campbell's events literally threw their shadows ahead of them.

clue.text: Mean to include one who uses 18 wrongly

indicators.note: including something means taking it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to imply is to mean or suggest
18 across is a lasso, and someone who throws a rope to catch cattle is a roper

explanation.surface: Someone who handles a lasso badly is called mean.
explanation.walkthrough: The lasso man sits inside the word for mean: IMP-ROPER-LY gives IMPROPERLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Improperly means in a way that is not correct or fitting, which is to say wrongly or incorrectly.

clue.text: Poor Nora, over-intellectual but decorative

indicators.note: something in poor shape is damaged, so the name that follows is knocked out of its order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
in a down clue, over places the first piece above this one; mental means of the intellect

explanation.surface: Poor Nora is too brainy, though she looks pretty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over-intellectual' reads as one hyphenated word; split it, 'over' sets the shuffled name above the word for intellectual in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ornamental serves as decoration or adornment rather than a practical purpose, the same sense as decorative.

clue.text: Gaiety intended by Miss Pecksniff, we Fear

indicators.note: the setter apologises in advance, owning that the match of sound is only approximate

blocks.note: Mercy Pecksniff in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit is called Merry; intended is meant

explanation.surface: A note of doubt about the cheerfulness a Dickens character means to show.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Pecksniff's daughters in Martin Chuzzlewit are Charity and Mercy, known as Cherry and Merry; Merry plus meant, said quickly, gives MERRIMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Merriment is cheerful fun and laughter, high spirits of the kind that gaiety also names.

clue.text: One-time beater lays down law

definitions.note: a description of what the person does, a verb phrase for a noun answer

blocks.note: ex means former
something that pounds or beats

explanation.surface: A former drummer or thug now dictates the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time beater' suggests a reformed bully, but it is just former plus something that pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: An expounder sets out and explains doctrine in detail, the role of someone who lays down the law to others.

clue.text: Much colder here in Paris — returning?

definitions.note: the answer is only colder; 'Much' colours the surface

blocks.note: the French word for here
re- is the prefix meaning back or again, the start of returning

explanation.surface: Someone back in Paris finds it much colder there than here.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose old-style clue: the French for here, then the back-again prefix turned round; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Icier is the comparative of icy, meaning colder, frozen over or frosty compared with something else.

clue.text: Right one at taking a lasso

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The right one is taking a lasso, perhaps a cowboy picking his rope.
explanation.walkthrough: A riata (or reata) is the Spanish-American name for a lariat.
explanation.definitionFit: A riata is the long rope with a running noose that cowhands throw to catch cattle, the same thing as a lasso.

clue.text: Being cheeky I am dismissed which is apposite

indicators.note: something dismissed is sent away, so those words leave the longer word

blocks.note: impertinent means rude or cheeky
I'm, the contraction of I am

explanation.surface: Someone being cheeky is sent away, which is only fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I'm from the front of the cheeky word and its opposite, PERTINENT, is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Pertinent means relevant and to the point, which is what an apposite remark is.

clue.text: Bard ordered to operate a lute

indicators.note: being ordered here means put into a new sequence, so the following letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A minstrel is commanded to play his lute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered to' reads as a command to the bard; the anagram signal is 'ordered' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A bard is a poet, and the poet appointed by the monarch to write for state occasions holds the official post in Britain.

clue.text: Passages from a play?

blocks.note: surface reading: extracts quoted from a drama
setter's reading: the ways out of a theatre, or actors leaving the stage as the stage directions say

explanation.walkthrough: Passages suggests excerpts of text; here they are routes out, and in a script the word marks a character leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The doors by which an audience leaves the theatre, and the stage directions for departing actors, are both ways out of a play.

clue.text: Sort of Kipling poem in a way

definitions.text: Sort of Kipling poem in a way

blocks.note: surface reading: something resembling a poem by Kipling
setter's reading: the word sounds like the end of Gunga Din

explanation.walkthrough: Gunga Din is Kipling's poem of the regimental water-carrier; the answer is nearly that title's last word, and 'by dint of' means by means of.
explanation.definitionFit: Dint means force or effort, used now almost only in the phrase meaning through the agency of, a way of achieving something.

clue.text: Some children identify with her

indicators.note: some of the following words means only a part of them, a run of letters inside

blocks.note: the run of letters across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Young readers relate to a favourite author.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Enid Blyton, the British author of the Famous Five and Noddy books, whom children identified with.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid is a woman's name, so any Enid can be referred to as her, and Blyton is the one the surface has in mind.

clue.text: Pity she was booked

blocks.note: first meaning: compassion, an old word surviving in ruthless
second meaning: a woman with a book of the Bible named after her

explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' suggests a reservation or a police charge; the Book of Ruth in the Old Testament is named for her.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth is an archaic noun for compassion or sorrow for another, the opposite of ruthlessness, so it means pity.

clue.text: Maid upset to share esteem

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the preceding word is jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
a ration is a fixed share or allowance

explanation.surface: A housemaid is upset at having to share, and keeps her self-respect.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiration is respect and warm approval for someone, which is what holding them in esteem means.

clue.text: Wall-squatter's yellow

blocks.note: surface reading: the cowardice of someone perched on a wall
setter's reading: the yellow inside Humpty Dumpty, the egg who sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme

explanation.walkthrough: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall and is drawn as an egg, so his yellow part is the centre of an egg.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow centre of an egg is the part that a broken Humpty Dumpty would spill when he had his great fall.

clue.text: Heavens! Venus may appear so curved?

definitions.text: Heavens! Venus may appear so curved?

blocks.clueFragment: Heavens! Venus may appear so curved?
blocks.note: surface reading: an exclamation at how shapely the goddess of love looks
setter's reading: the planet in the heavens shows phases like the Moon, sometimes as a thin curved sliver

explanation.walkthrough: Venus as goddess suggests a curvy figure; as a planet in the night sky it shows phases and can look like a new moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Through a telescope the planet near the Sun shows only a thin lit sliver, shaped like the new moon, and that shape is the adjective.
